newsitem.title: DENMARK: Crucial EU battle opens in Danish court.
newsitem.headline: Crucial EU battle opens in Danish court.

text.p: COPENHAGEN, May 26 Reuter) - A Danish court on Monday started hearing a challenge to the legality of Denmark's European Union treaties which legal experts say could end the country's EU membership under the present terms.
The High Court case is scheduled to run until mid-June but legal experts say that an eventual Supreme Court appeal could delay a definitive verdict until the end of the year or beyond.

The plaintiffs, a non-partisan group of 10 Danes, argue that since joining the EU in 1973 Denmark has ceded national authority to European Union institutions in breach of its own constitution. But they see little chance of winning at the High Court stage.
"The case will only be decided in the Supreme Court. The High Court is too conservative to find in our favour," group member Nicolas Fischer told Reuters in court.

The daily Berlingske Tidende appeared to agree, citing High Court pre-trial rulings against the plaintiffs on questions of what evidence is admissible and saying that the court wanted to stay clear of the case's political overtones.

"One could argue, somewhat cynically, that there is no point in being concerned about the so-called constitution case beginning today in the High Court until the Supreme Court judges get their hands on it," the paper wrote.
The Danish bond market, which became somewhat jittery during pre-trial hearings last year, ignored Monday's opening of the trial proper.
"Only when the (High Court) judgement is announced do we expect a reaction," a dealer said.

The group of 10, calling themselves the Constitution Committee, have sought to have confidential government papers, dating back to Denmark's EU accession and beyond, introduced as evidence but have been repeatedly refused.
The committee's lawyers will argue that the treaties do not sufficiently define the extent to which the European Court and other EU institutions may override national bodies.
The Danish constitution's article 20 states that national powers may only be delegated to international organisations "within a specified limit".

The centre-left coalition government believes its case is watertight and lawyers from both sides say that state attorneys' task has been eased by rulings that the case should be limited to events since the 1992 Maastricht treaty.
Independent legal experts generally see a government win as the most likely outcome, but by no means certain.
A defeat would force Denmark into the unwieldy and potentially destabilising process of renegotiating its EU treaties or the complex and difficult task of rewriting the national constitution.
The government wants a quick decision, as the case casts a shadow over Danish ratification of a revised European Union treaty to be signed at the next summit, in Amsterdam next month.
Danes, traditionally cool toward European integration, rejected the Maastricht Treaty outright in a 1992 referendum.
Voters grudgingly approved the treaty the following year on condition that Denmark opt out of economic and monetary union and joint defence, policing and asylum policies.
